stops.name: Kingston upon Thames: the birth of Edward Muggeridge
stops.campa: On 9 April 1830, in the market town of Kingston upon Thames, Edward James Muggeridge is born above the family grain-and-coal business on the river. His father John barges corn along the Thames; the boy grows among sacks and scales and the slow water. He is quick, restless, ambitious beyond the wharf. Later he will Saxon-spell himself Eadweard, reclaiming the old form carved on the Coronation Stone where Saxon kings were crowned in this very town, and take the surname Muybridge, the ancient one, he insists. The town that will bury him first sets him loose.

stops.name: New Orleans: the book agent lands in America
stops.campa: Around twenty, hungry for the New World, he sails for New York and enters the book trade. By January 1855 he has come down to New Orleans as a travelling book agent, carrying illustrated Shakespeares and fine bindings through a country still half wilderness. He is a salesman of images and words, an Englishman with a plan and an accent, working his way toward the golden coast where a new city is rising on the far Pacific. The tools of his second life, the printed picture, the sequence of plates, are already in his hands.

stops.name: San Francisco: Muygridge, bookseller of Montgomery Street
stops.campa: By 1856 he has settled in booming San Francisco and set up as a bookseller on Montgomery Street, agent for the London Printing and Publishing Company. He sells engravings and lithographs to a gold-rush city that wants pictures of the wider world. He is prosperous, dapper, known about town. He has not yet touched a camera. Then, in the spring of 1860, he sells the business to his brother, means to sail home to England to buy stock, and takes the overland stage east across the continent. The road to Fort Smith will change everything.
stops.quote: I have this day sold to my brother, Thomas S. Muybridge
stops.quote_source: Notice in the San Francisco Bulletin, May 1860

stops.name: North of Fort Worth, Texas: the runaway stagecoach
stops.campa: On 22 July 1860, on the Butterfield Overland Mail road above Fort Worth, the horses of the Concord stage bolt and cannot be held. The coach smashes into a tree; the driver and one passenger are killed outright, the rest flung and broken. Muybridge is thrown headlong and strikes his skull against a rock. Everything goes dark. In this instant, the tradition holds, a tradesman dies and an artist is born: the injury that will loose the strange, obsessive, brilliant man who chases the invisible instant. Motion has nearly killed him. He will spend his life arresting it.

stops.name: Fort Smith, Arkansas: waking with nine days lost
stops.campa: He wakes in a hospital bed at Fort Smith with no memory of the nine days since he ate supper at a wayside cabin 150 miles back. His head splits; his vision is doubled, his hearing dimmed, taste and smell gone, his mind confused. It is said his black hair turns grey in three days. The physicians can do little on the frontier. The change is not only physical: those who knew the smooth bookseller find him afterward eccentric, risk-taking, prone to rages and to genius; a different man walks out of Fort Smith than the one the coach threw down.

stops.name: London: Sir William Gull and the years of shadow
stops.campa: He returns to England to heal, and is treated by Sir William Gull, physician to the Queen's household, who advises open air, riding, and no strain. For several years Muybridge nearly vanishes from the record: Paris, patents, small inventions, a washing machine, a printing plate. Somewhere in this shadow-time he learns the wet-collodion craft of photography, the sun-drawing that will be his instrument. When he steps back into the light in San Francisco he is no longer Muggeridge the bookseller. He signs his negatives with the name of the sun.

stops.name: San Francisco: the return of Helios, sun-drawer
stops.campa: On 13 February 1867 Muybridge is back in San Francisco, reborn as a photographer under the pseudonym Helios, the Greek sun, for photography is drawing with light. He builds a portable darkroom into a light two-wheeled carriage and paints on its back the name Helios' Flying Studio. With it he can carry the chemistry of the wet plate into any wilderness, coating, exposing, and developing before the collodion dries. The instant he once nearly died beneath, he will now hunt and pin to glass. The man who lost nine days sets out to capture single seconds.

stops.name: Yosemite Valley: the first great views, 1867
stops.campa: From June to November 1867 Helios climbs into Yosemite and makes seventy-two large views and more than a hundred stereographs of the cathedral valley: Yosemite Falls thundering, El Capitan's sheer face, the Merced mirror-still. He lashes himself to the edges of cliffs for the vantage; he waits on the light. The prints astonish San Francisco and make his name overnight. Where Carleton Watkins had gone before, Muybridge goes higher, stranger, more dramatic: inventing clouds later in the darkroom, arranging the sublime. The wilderness photographer is the same eye that will later dissect a stride.

stops.name: Sitka, Alaska: photographing the new Territory
stops.campa: In 1868, the year after the purchase of Alaska, the United States government sends Muybridge north to photograph the newly acquired Territory. He sails to Sitka and the Alexander Archipelago, documenting the fortress-town, the rain-forest coast, the totems and houses of the Tlingit. His views of Alaska help fix the far corner of the young continent in the American imagination. The camera that will one day map the geometry of a running body first maps the edges of an empire: glaciers, harbors, the last frontier of the sun's drawing.

stops.name: Point Reyes: the lighthouses of the Pacific coast
stops.campa: In 1871 the United States Lighthouse Board commissions Muybridge to photograph the beacons of the Pacific coast, from the fog-wrapped tower at Point Reyes to the lights of the Farallones and the Oregon shore. He records the lonely lamps that guard the shipping lanes, the keepers, the surf below sheer bluffs. The same year, on 20 May, he marries Flora Shallcross Stone, a divorcée of twenty-one, half his age. Light and marriage arrive together. Both, in the years to come, will be undone: one lover, one bullet.

stops.name: Yosemite Valley: the mammoth plates of 1872
stops.campa: In 1872 Muybridge returns to Yosemite and makes fifty-one mammoth plates on 18-by-22-inch glass, the largest wilderness photographs yet attempted in America. He hauls the enormous cameras and the flying darkroom up to viewpoints no one has photographed, dangling over precipices, felling trees that block his sight-lines. The Bradley & Rulofson prints crown him the foremost landscape photographer of the West. In this same year Leland Stanford, railroad king and horseman, hears of the wizard who can make the sun obey, and sends for him with a question about a galloping horse.

stops.name: Sacramento: Stanford's question and the first trials, 1873
stops.campa: Leland Stanford, former governor, builder of the Central Pacific, breeder of trotters, poses in 1872 the question that will consume Muybridge: when a horse runs, is there an instant when all four hooves leave the ground together? No eye can settle it; the legs blur. Horsemen argue; Stanford, they say, has a wager on it. In 1873, at Union Park racetrack in Sacramento, Muybridge makes the first attempts, trying to freeze the trotter Occident with a single fast shutter against a white sheet. The images are faint ghosts, but they hint that the unsupported instant is real, and that the camera can prove it.
